# An HTTP API with `asynchttpserver`

Building an HTTP server sounds like a large project. With `std/asynchttpserver`, a small server is
about a dozen lines, and every part comes from the standard library. What makes server code hard to
test is not the socket, it is the handler tangled up with the socket.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can tell `HttpCode` and `HttpMethod` apart, write simple routes, read a JSON
body and return JSON, read a *query string* with `std/uri`, start a server with `newAsyncHttpServer`
and `serve`, and read the `has to be used (or discarded)` message when you forget `await` on
`respond`.
:::

## Status, method, and headers

Before touching a socket, get to know the shared types: `HttpCode`, `HttpMethod`, and `HttpHeaders`.
They all come from `std/httpcore`, the module used by both the client and the server side. Save the
example as `main.nim`, then run `nim c -r main.nim`.

```{.nim}
import std/httpcore

var headers = newHttpHeaders()
headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"

echo Http200
echo Http404
echo HttpGet
echo headers["Content-Type"]
```

```{.txt}
200 OK
404 Not Found
GET
application/json
```

`Http200` is a value of `HttpCode`, a `distinct` type whose range is limited to 0 through 599.
`httpcore` provides `$` for it, so `echo Http200` prints `"200 OK"` instead of a bare number. The
`.int` conversion gives back just the number, and is used later to build compact output.
`HttpMethod` is an `enum`: `HttpGet` carries the text `GET`, `HttpPost` carries `POST`, and so on.

`HttpHeaders` is a map whose keys ignore case. Writing `headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"`
adds one entry; reading it back with different capitalization still finds that entry.

## Simple routes and a pure handler

A single handler receives the method, the path, and the body, then decides the code and the reply.
Separate that decision from the socket, and the result can be tested as an ordinary function. Save
the next piece, then run it the same way.

```{.nim}
import std/[httpcore, json]

type Reply = tuple[code: HttpCode, body: string]

proc dispatch(httpMethod: HttpMethod, path: string, body: string): Reply =
  case path
  of "/health":
    (Http200, """{"status":"ok"}""")
  of "/items":
    if httpMethod != HttpPost:
      (Http400, """{"error":"POST required"}""")
    else:
      let payload = parseJson(body)
      (Http200, $(%*{"name": payload["name"].getStr}))
  else:
    (Http404, """{"error":"not found"}""")

let requests = [
  (HttpGet, "/health", ""),
  (HttpPost, "/items", """{"name":"book"}"""),
  (HttpGet, "/items", ""),
  (HttpGet, "/missing", ""),
]

for (httpMethod, path, body) in requests:
  let reply = dispatch(httpMethod, path, body)
  echo reply.code.int, " ", reply.body
```

```{.txt}
200 {"status":"ok"}
200 {"name":"book"}
400 {"error":"POST required"}
404 {"error":"not found"}
```

Routes are matched with `case path`. The `/items` path accepts `HttpPost` only; another method gets
`Http400`, meaning the client request is wrong. An unknown path gets `Http404`. The distinction
matters: `Http400` blames the request, `Http404` says the route does not exist.

The JSON body is read with `parseJson` from `std/json`. A field is taken with `payload["name"]`,
then `getStr` turns it into a `string`. To reply, `%*{...}` builds JSON directly and `$` turns it
into text: `$(%*{"name": ...})`. Because `dispatch` calls `parseJson`, it is declared as a `proc`,
not a `func`. `parseJson` has side effects according to the compiler, and a `func` refuses to call
it.

The parameter is named `httpMethod`, not `method`, because `method` is a Nim keyword.

## Query string

Data that is not required to travel in the body usually rides along in the URL. `std/uri` splits it
apart.

```{.nim}
import std/uri

let target = parseUri("/search?q=nim+lang&page=2")

echo "path: ", target.path
echo "query: ", target.query
for key, value in decodeQuery(target.query):
  echo key, " = ", value
```

```{.txt}
path: /search
query: q=nim+lang&page=2
q = nim lang
page = 2
```

`parseUri` breaks a URL into its parts: `.path`, `.query`, `.hostname`, and others. The `query` part
is still raw text. The `decodeQuery` iterator splits on `&`, then parses each `key=value` pair. Note
`q`: the plus sign becomes a space, because in a *query string* `+` really does stand for a space.
The values it prints are already decoded and ready to use.

## From `Request` to the handler

When the server calls a handler, it hands over a `Request`: an object carrying the method, URL,
headers, and body. The example builds one `Request` by hand to look at its fields without touching
the network.

```{.nim}
import std/[asynchttpserver, httpcore, uri]

let request = Request(reqMethod: HttpGet, url: parseUri("/items/7"))

func describe(req: Request): string =
  $req.reqMethod & " " & req.url.path

echo describe(request)
```

```{.txt}
GET /items/7
```

`reqMethod` is an `HttpMethod`, and `url` is the same `Uri` that `parseUri` produces. Since
`Request` is an ordinary object, it can be built inside a test: just fill the fields you need. That
is why a pure handler is easy to test while the socket does not have to run at all.

## Starting the server

Now connect the pure handler to a real server. `newAsyncHttpServer` creates the server, `serve` binds
it to a port and calls `handle` for every request. `respond` sends the reply.

```{.nim}
import std/[asynchttpserver, asyncdispatch, httpcore, uri]

func dispatch(httpMethod: HttpMethod, path: string,
              body: string): tuple[code: HttpCode, body: string] =
  case path
  of "/health":
    (Http200, """{"status":"ok"}""")
  else:
    (Http404, """{"error":"not found"}""")

proc handle(req: Request): Future[void] {.async.} =
  let (code, body) = dispatch(req.reqMethod, req.url.path, req.body)
  let headers = newHttpHeaders({"Content-Type": "application/json"})
  await req.respond(code, body, headers)

proc main() {.async.} =
  let server = newAsyncHttpServer()
  await server.serve(Port(8080), handle)

# The real program ends by starting the event loop: waitFor main()
for (httpMethod, path) in [(HttpGet, "/health"), (HttpGet, "/nope")]:
  let reply = dispatch(httpMethod, path, "")
  echo reply.code.int, " ", reply.body
```

```{.txt}
200 {"status":"ok"}
404 {"error":"not found"}
```

`handle` is marked `{.async.}` because `respond` returns a `Future[void]`, and the result must be
written with `await`. The `main` procedure builds the server, then calls `serve`. The real server is
not started here: the example calls `dispatch` directly so the output stays fixed. In a real program
the last line is `waitFor main()`, which runs the event loop.

Once the server is running, test it with an ordinary command line tool:

```bash
$ curl -s http://localhost:8080/health
{"status":"ok"}
$ curl -s http://localhost:8080/nope
{"error":"not found"}
```

## Intentional error: forgetting `await` on `respond`

The first mistake almost everyone makes: calling `respond` without `await`.

```{.nim}
import std/[asynchttpserver, asyncdispatch, httpcore]

proc handle(req: Request) {.async.} =
  req.respond(Http200, "ok")
  echo "sent"
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(4, 6) Error: expression 'respond(req, Http200, "ok", nil)' is of type 'Future[system.void]' and has to be used (or discarded)
```

The message has two parts. The first names the type of the call's result: `Future[system.void]`, not
`void`. The second offers two choices, use the value or discard it on purpose. Since we do want to
wait for the reply to be sent, the answer is `await`. The correct spelling is
`await req.respond(Http200, "ok")`. The compiler also marks the line where `{.async.}` is used, a
sign that the problem sits inside the async procedure.

## Why the handler is kept apart from the socket

The split above is not decoration. A handler that takes data and returns data can be tested without
a port, without a network, and without waiting. Its output is always the same, so it can serve as a
verified example. The socket is only a thin layer that forwards requests. Keeping that layer as thin
as possible is a habit worth carrying as the API grows.

## Exercises

1. Add a `/version` route to `dispatch` that returns `{"version":"1"}` with `Http200`, then print
   the reply.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/httpcore

   func status(path: string): HttpCode =
     case path
     of "/ready": Http200
     else: Http404

   for path in ["/ready", "/other"]:
     echo status(path).int
   ```
3. Write from scratch: a handler that reads `page` from the *query string* and returns it as JSON,
   for example `{"page":"2"}`.
4. The code below fails to compile. Fix it, then explain its message:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/[asynchttpserver, asyncdispatch, httpcore]

   proc handle(req: Request) {.async.} =
     await req.respond("ok", Http200)
   ```
5. When is a request answered with `Http400`, and when with `Http404`? Give one example of each.

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- `std/httpcore` provides `HttpCode`, `HttpMethod`, and `HttpHeaders` for both sides.
- A pure `dispatch` separates route decisions from the socket, so it can be tested with fixed output.
- A JSON body is read with `parseJson` and answered with `%*` followed by `$`.
- `parseUri` and `decodeQuery` pull values out of a *query string*.
- `newAsyncHttpServer` and `serve` connect the handler; `respond` must be called with `await`.
